{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-sc-d","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"4ccc2942f9a669b0e996b84d7c45f298840414bf7d2fd89ed674245c840a2d8d","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-sc-class-d:lineage:14","source_registry_sha256":"61c32f86a25e3c021742b3c9ddf64a97709817dd75a19df6d2b69eac0a40c4f1","source_liveness_sha256":"feb7871590284d2a19ab0509ff65b48154ba15e637a6ec9b839f55a72736ffdb"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Fitness to drive: vision, fatigue, distraction, aggression, alcohol and drugs, emotions and aging","heading":"C — Vision rules and screening, fatigue, distractions and the hands-free law, aggressive driving, alcohol and other drugs, emotions and tips for older drivers","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Vision rules and screening, fatigue, distractions and the hands-free law, aggressive driving, alcohol and other drugs, emotions and tips for older drivers
Knowledge domain: the physical and mental condition a South Carolina driver needs, from vision standards and screening rules to fatigue, distraction, aggressive driving, the legal and physical effects of alcohol and other drugs, emotional state and the warning signs for older drivers.

FACT_ID: sec04-F01 | anchor: A01
Safe driving depends on good health and making correct decisions, and the manual calls driving one of the riskiest activities you may choose. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec04-F02 | anchor: A01
Without clear vision you struggle to identify traffic and road conditions, spot trouble and respond in time, so regular eye checks by a licensed eye care professional are advised. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec04-F03 | anchor: A01
If corrective lenses are required, always wear them when driving and avoid dark or tinted lenses at night, because they cut the light you need to see. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec04-F04 | anchor: A01
Drivers who use bioptic telescopic lenses must send the Low Vision Acuity Screening form 412-LV to the SCDMV Driver Improvement unit every year. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec04-F05 | anchor: A02
Vision can be tested at a branch with an orthorater, a device that checks how well you read at a distance, or by a licensed eye care professional. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec04-F06 | anchor: A02
A licensed eye care professional must test you if you fail the SCDMV vision test or choose not to be tested at the branch. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec04-F07 | anchor: A02
SC-licensed eye care professionals submit the Certificate of Vision Examination online, while out-of-state professionals complete SCDMV Form 412-NC. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec04-F08 | anchor: A02
Vision screening is required for a first SC permit or license, to remove corrective lens restriction code A, for renewals of a license or permit since October 1, 2020, and when surrendering an out-of-state license. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec04-F09 | anchor: A02
From May 18, 2024, standard vision screening certificates stay valid for 36 months. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec04-F10 | anchor: A02
The minimum vision standard is no stricter than 20/40 corrected in one eye. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec04-F11 | anchor: A02
If you meet the standard only with glasses or contacts, a restriction is added to your permit or license, and driving without those lenses is unlawful. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec04-F12 | anchor: A03
If your vision improves so lenses are no longer needed, you provide a new vision certificate from a licensed eye care professional and renew the license to remove the restriction. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec04-F13 | anchor: A03
Fatigue is physical or mental tiredness from strain, repetitive tasks, illness or lack of sleep, and it can affect vision and slow decisions. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec04-F14 | anchor: A03
Most people need 7 to 9 hours of sleep a day to stay properly alert during waking hours. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec04-F15 | anchor: A03
On long trips, plan to stop about every 100 miles or 2 hours. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec04-F16 | anchor: A03
Other trip tips are bringing a companion to watch your driving, checking medicine labels for drowsiness warnings and avoiding alcohol and other drugs before or while driving. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec04-F17 | anchor: A03
If you begin to feel tired, pull off at the next exit or rest area and nap for 15 to 20 minutes, or stop somewhere to sleep for the night. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec04-F18 | anchor: A03
Try not to drive late at night, and remember that plenty of rest is the best defense against fatigue. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec04-F19 | anchor: A04
A distraction is anything that pulls your attention from driving, and mental distractions are as dangerous as taking your eyes off the road or hands off the wheel. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec04-F20 | anchor: A04
In SC it is unlawful to use a wireless electronic communication device while driving if it requires either hand, under SC Code §56-5-3890. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec04-F21 | anchor: A04
While driving, avoid arguments and emotional conversations with passengers, avoid eating, make sure children are buckled properly and keep pets in a carrier or portable kennel. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec04-F22 | anchor: A04
Aggressive driving is an intentional act by a driver that endangers other people or property. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec04-F23 | anchor: A05
Typical aggressive driving behaviors are speeding, tailgating, unsafe lane changes, signaling improperly or not at all, and ignoring traffic control devices. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec04-F24 | anchor: A05
Alcohol and other impairing drugs are involved in about 40% of traffic collisions that kill someone each year. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec04-F25 | anchor: A05
Drivers under 21 may not legally buy, possess or drink alcohol, and every state has zero tolerance or similar laws for drivers under 21. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec04-F26 | anchor: A05
Alcohol and impairing drugs hit new drivers harder because they are still learning complex skills. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec04-F27 | anchor: A05
Alcohol and other impairing drugs reduce judgment, the brain's quick use of stored experience and knowledge when facing a new problem. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec04-F28 | anchor: A06
Alcohol blurs vision, slows focusing, can cause double vision and weakens your judgment of distance, speed and other vehicles' movement, with vision affected at 0.02 percent BAC for every driver. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0037]

FACT_ID: sec04-F29 | anchor: A06
Alcohol also reduces your ability to tell colors apart and slows your reaction time. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0037]

FACT_ID: sec04-F30 | anchor: A06
Impairment begins with the first drink, and anyone with even one drink in the bloodstream could be arrested for driving under the influence. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0037]

FACT_ID: sec04-F31 | anchor: A06
BAC, blood alcohol concentration, is the percentage of alcohol relative to the amount of blood in your body. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0037]

FACT_ID: sec04-F32 | anchor: A06
A DUI or DUAC conviction, a BAC of 0.15 percent or more, or refusing implied consent testing may lead to suspension of your license and driving privileges. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0037]

FACT_ID: sec04-F33 | anchor: A06
You can be convicted of impaired driving with a BAC of only 0.05, or lower when combined with drugs, including prescription and over-the-counter medicines. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0037]

FACT_ID: sec04-F34 | anchor: A06
A driver under 21 who registers a BAC of 0.02 percent or more has the privilege to drive suspended immediately for at least three months. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0037]

FACT_ID: sec04-F35 | anchor: A07
A driver under 21 who refuses the test for intoxicants immediately loses driving privileges for at least six months. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0038]

FACT_ID: sec04-F36 | anchor: A07
Under SC's implied consent law, getting a license means you have agreed in advance to a lawful breath, blood or urine test if suspected of impaired driving, and refusing can cost you your license. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0038]

FACT_ID: sec04-F37 | anchor: A07
Implied consent laws differ by state, and the law of the state where you are arrested applies, not the state that issued your license. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0038]

FACT_ID: sec04-F38 | anchor: A07
Many prescription and over-the-counter drugs can affect driving as much as alcohol or worse. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0038]

FACT_ID: sec04-F39 | anchor: A08
Over-the-counter medicines for headaches, colds, allergies or nerves can cause drowsiness, while pep pills, uppers and diet pills can cause nervousness, dizziness, poor concentration and vision problems. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec04-F40 | anchor: A08
Check the label of any medicine for warnings before taking it, and ask a doctor or pharmacist if you are unsure whether it is safe to drive. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec04-F41 | anchor: A08
A conviction in SC for driving under the influence of drugs is treated the same as a DUI or DUAC conviction. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec04-F42 | anchor: A08
Never drink alcohol while taking other drugs, because they can multiply alcohol's effects or add effects of their own. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec04-F43 | anchor: A09
Strong emotions interfere with thinking, attention and processing information, so if you are angry or worried, cool off first, perhaps with a short walk or nap, or let someone else drive. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec04-F44 | anchor: A09
Aging can dull hearing and eyesight, slow judgment and reaction in emergencies, and leave an older driver unaware of new rules and regulations. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec04-F45 | anchor: A10
If two or three of the listed warning signs apply to an older driver, it may be time to change driving habits or stop driving, and a doctor may refer the driver for an assessment by an SCDMV examiner or another trained medical professional. [A10]
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec04-F46 | anchor: A10
Warning signs include needing several tries to parallel park, confusing objects such as a hydrant and a small child, long-lasting headlight glare discomfort, trouble keeping pace with traffic and slow starts at green lights. [A10]
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec04-F47 | anchor: A10
More warning signs are frequent minor scrapes or dents, missing STOP and highway signs, confusion in unexpected situations and trouble making out objects a few feet away. [A10]
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec04-F48 | anchor: A11
Trouble judging how far away an approaching vehicle is, or seeing the sides of the road while looking straight ahead, are also warning signs. [A11]
Source: [A11 -> pdf-0042]

Misconceptions: tinted lenses at night reduce the light you need even if they seem to cut glare; mental distraction is as dangerous as looking away from the road; a driver can be convicted of impaired driving at a BAC as low as point zero five, or lower when drugs are involved; implied consent follows the state of arrest, not the state of licensing; over-the-counter medicine can impair as much as alcohol.
Mnemonics: sleep seven to nine, stop every hundred miles or two hours, nap fifteen to twenty minutes; for under twenty-one, a reading of point zero two or more means at least three months, and refusing means at least six months.
Glossary: orthorater means the branch device that tests distance vision; bioptic telescopic lenses means special low-vision lenses that need a yearly SCDMV form; BAC means blood alcohol concentration; DUAC means driving with an unlawful alcohol concentration; implied consent means the advance agreement to alcohol testing that comes with a license; zero tolerance means no alcohol allowed in the circulatory system of young drivers.
Dynamic facts: vision form numbers, the certificate validity period and the screening rules have changed over time and can change again; confirm them on the SCDMV website.
